newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan sees offshore stock-index futures in April.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan sees offshore stock-index futures in April.

text.p: Taiwan officials voiced support on Wednesday for the lifting of a ban on local trading of offshore Taiwan stock-index futures now that a long-awaited futures law has been passed.
Finance Minister Paul Chiu told parliament's finance panel that he would make a formal announcement on the ban in April.
"We will decide on the trading of offshore stock-index futures by the end of April," Chiu said. "The Finance Ministry is leaning toward allowing it. We have a positive attitude."
Aides to Chiu said the trading of Taiwan stock-index futures launched in Chicago and Singapore in January would be legal as soon as an announcement is made, but would need further review.
Taiwan's central bank expressed "cautious support" for the liberalisation on March 1 -- before parliament adopted the long-delayed Futures Trading Law on Tuesday.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), which has criticised the offshore exchanges for the premature launch of Taiwan-linked contracts and threatened to interfere with their operation, is subordinate to the Finance Ministry and would be expected to support a liberalisation.
With the new law in place, Taiwan promoters are expected to open the island's own futures exchange, which would offer Taiwan stock-index futures -- but not before October.

Liberalising access to offshore contracts as soon as April would open a window of opportunity of several months for the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) and Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX), which have been pressing for access to Taiwan's still-untapped futures market.

The CME and SIMEX launched futures on January 9 linked to Taiwan's stock market performance, although Taipei has not allowed either to peg its contracts to the proprietary TAIEX index compiled by the Taiwan Stock Exchange.

The CME and SIMEX launched their contracts in defiance of the watchdog commission, which has withheld cooperation and even threatened to block CME and SIMEX access to stock price data essential to the indexes underlying their contracts.

Local futures houses are allowed to sell a range of overseas futures contracts, but officials have refused to allow trading of the CME and SIMEX contracts -- to date, the only futures linked directly to Taiwan's own financial performance.

Many local investors are believed to be skirting the ban by placing orders through offshore brokers, a practice that has compounded pressure on Taiwan to launch its own futures or at least to allow access to the offshore Taiwan index contracts.
SEC officials have said their main concern in reviewing the liberalisation is whether the offshore contracts are traded at volumes large enough to ensure healthy market liquidity.
Although trading of the SIMEX contracts has been more robust, commission officials believe both offshore exchanges have acceptable levels of trading volume.
"The liquidity of both the Singapore and Chicago Taiwan stock-index futures is fine," one commission official said.
The official declined to elaborate on what liquidity level is required for the SEC to approve local trading.
